\textbf{Supplementary Equations: Models of variant nowcasting}

\begin{center}
\fbox{\begin{minipage}{0.94\linewidth}
\textbf{Supplementary Box 1. Logistic growth}

\smallskip
\textit{Adapted from Chen et al., 2021 and Althaus et al., 2021}

\medskip
\textbf{Sequence observation process}
\[
n_v(t) \sim \text{Binomial}\left(N(t),\ p_v(t)\right) \tag{S1}
\]
Where the number of observations of our variant of interest (for example, PANGO lineage B.1.1.7) at time $t$ is $n_v(t)$ and is binomially distributed, $N(t)$ is the number of sequences collected at $t$ and $p_v(t)$ is the expected proportion of sequences at $t$ that are variant $v$ (equivalently, the probability that a given sequence is variant $v$).

\medskip
\textbf{Variant frequency logistic model}
\[
p_v(t) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\left(-\beta_v (t - t_0)\right)} \tag{S2}
\]
Where $p_v(t)$ is the proportion of sequences that are variant $v$ at time $t$, and $\beta_v$ is the variant's logistic growth rate relative to all other background variants and $t_0$ is the sigmoid midpoint. 
\end{minipage}}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\fbox{\begin{minipage}{0.94\linewidth}
\textbf{Supplementary Box 2. Multinomial growth}

\smallskip
\textit{Adapted from Abousamra et al., 2024}

\medskip
\textbf{Sequence observation process}
\[
\left(n_1(t), \dots, n_K(t)\right) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(N(t);\ p_1(t), \dots, p_K(t)\right) \tag{S3}
\]
Where $n_k(t)$ is the number of sequences of variant $k$ at time $t$, for each of the $K$ variants ($k = 1, \dots, K$), $N(t)$ is the number of sequences collected at $t$, and $p_k(t)$ is the expected proportion of sequences at $t$ that are variant $k$ (equivalently, the probability that a given sequence is variant $k$). The variant of interest $v$ is one of these $K$ variants.

\medskip
\textbf{Variant frequency multinomial model}
\[
p_v(t) = \frac{\exp(f_{0,v} + \beta_v t)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \exp(f_{0,k} + \beta_k t)} \tag{S4}
\]
Where $p_v(t)$ is the expected proportion of sequences that are variant $v$ at time $t$, and $\beta_v$ is the logistic growth rate of variant $v$ relative to the reference variant, $f_{0,v}$ and $f_{0,k}$ are the log initial frequencies of variants $v$ and $k$, respectively, relative to a reference variant, which has $\beta$ and $f_0$ set to zero.
\end{minipage}}
\end{center}

\begin{center}
\fbox{\begin{minipage}{0.94\linewidth}
\textbf{Supplementary Box 3. Transmission advantage}

\medskip
Assuming a fixed generation time of $g$, the transmission advantage, or $\Delta_v$, is the $R_t$ of the novel variant over all other variants, i.e. $R_{t,\text{novel}}/R_{t,\text{background}}$. 
\[
\Delta_v = \exp{(\beta_v g)} = \frac{R_{t,\text{novel}}}{R_{t,\text{background}}} \tag{S5}
\]
Where $g$ is usually a generation time point estimate, in the same time units as $\beta_v$, and is shared by the novel and reference or background variants. In the multinomial model, the transmission advantage becomes $R_{t,\text{variant }k}/R_{t,\text{reference variant}}$.
\end{minipage}}
\end{center}
